key_terms.meaning: Program that reads commands, interprets them, and starts other programs; also a programming language.
The portable Unix shell by Stephen Bourne; standard syntax for scripts.
Bourne Again SHell; successor to sh with extensions such as arrays and [[ ]].
Named string in the shell; assigned as name=value with no spaces around =.
Rules using backslash, single quotes and double quotes that control expansion and word splitting.
Preserve every character literally; no variable expansion inside.
Allow $, backticks and backslash expansion but stop word splitting and globbing.
Number 0–255 returned by a command; 0 is success or true, non-zero is failure or false.
Runs commands when a command list returns status 0; optional elif and else branches follow.
Matches a word against patterns and runs the first matching branch.
while, until and for repeat commands; while runs while status is 0, until runs until status is 0, for iterates over words.
Named group of commands run in the current shell; called like a command.
$1, $2, ... and $# inside a script or function; $0 is the script or shell name.
Small non-negative integer for an open stream; 0 is stdin, 1 is stdout and 2 is stderr.
Shell action that connects a file descriptor to a file or another descriptor, for example >, < or 2>.
Redirection << word feeds following lines to stdin until a line equal to word.
Operator | connects stdout of the left command to stdin of the right command.
Program that reads stdin, transforms data and writes stdout; used in pipelines.
grep selects lines by pattern; sed edits a stream line by line; awk processes records and fields.
set -e exits on an unchecked failure; set -x prints commands before running them.

takeaways: The shell is both a command interpreter and a programming language; sh gives portable syntax and Bash adds extensions.
Shell variables store strings, and quoting decides expansion, literal text and word splitting.
Exit status is the basis of shell decisions: 0 means true or success, non-zero means false or failure.
if, case and loops choose which commands run and repeat work over lists or input.
Functions group commands, receive positional parameters, return an exit status and send data through stdout.
File descriptors 0, 1 and 2 plus redirection and here-documents connect scripts to files and logs.
Pipes chain filters so stdout of one command becomes stdin of the next command.
grep, sed and awk cover line selection, stream editing and field summaries; debugging uses status checks, set -e, set -x, trap and logs.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine syntax with working script fragments: quoting and variables, exit-status control flow, functions and arguments, redirection and pipes, grep/sed/awk pipelines, and defensive error handling.

bank.q: Explain the shell as both a command interpreter and a programming language. Compare the Bourne shell (sh) and Bash in portability and features.
outline: Shell reads a command line, expands words, executes commands and starts programs.
Shell language includes variables, control flow, functions and redirection.
sh is the portable POSIX base with small standard syntax.
Bash is its successor and adds arrays, [[ ]], brace expansion and process substitution.
Scripts choose #!/bin/sh or #!/bin/bash according to needed features.

bank.q: Explain shell variables and quoting. Show how unquoted, single-quoted and double-quoted values differ for $name and word splitting.
outline: Assignment is name=value with no spaces around =.
$name expands to the stored string.
Unquoted expansion splits on IFS and can glob.
Single quotes keep every character literal.
Double quotes expand variables but stop splitting and globbing.
Backslash escapes a single character.

bank.q: Define exit status. Explain how if and loops use exit status, and how case selects branches by pattern.
outline: Exit status 0 means success or true; 1–255 means failure or false.
if command; then ... uses the status of a command list.
while runs while its condition returns 0; until runs until it returns 0.
case matches a word against patterns and runs the first match.
$? holds the last command status.

bank.q: Explain shell functions and positional parameters. How does a function return an exit status and how does it send data to the caller?
outline: Function name() { commands; } runs in the current shell.
$1, $2, $# and $@ work inside the function.
return n sets the function exit status.
exit ends the whole shell or script.
Data returns through stdout and command substitution.
local limits a variable to the function.

bank.q: Write a shell script that reads a file line by line, skips empty lines, counts non-empty lines and prints the count. Use a loop and input redirection.
outline: while IFS= read -r line; do ... done < file.
[ -n "$line" ] tests for a non-empty line.
count=$((count+1)) increments the counter.
printf prints the final count.
Variables are quoted to avoid splitting.

bank.q: Write a shell script that creates a configuration file with a here-document and sends error messages to a log file while normal output stays on the terminal.
outline: cat > config <<'EOF' writes literal lines until EOF.
Quoting the delimiter stops expansion.
command 2>> error.log appends stderr to the log.
stdout remains on the terminal by default.
exec 2>>log can redirect errors for the rest of the script.

bank.q: Use a pipeline of grep, sed and awk to read a log file, keep lines containing ERROR, remove a timestamp prefix, and print the count of messages per user field.
outline: grep 'ERROR' log selects matching lines.
sed removes the prefix with a substitution.
awk '{count[$NF]++} END {for (u in count) print u, count[u]}' summarises fields.
Pipes connect stdout to stdin at each stage.
Patterns are quoted to protect special characters.

bank.q: Write a shell function that validates whether its first argument is a positive integer and returns 0 or 1. Call it for two values and print a message based on status.
outline: Function reads $1.
case "$1" in ''|*[!0-9]*) return 1;; esac rejects non-digits.
[ "$1" -gt 0 ] checks positivity.
return 0 or return 1 sets status.
if validate "$x"; then ... tests the status.
The function sends no data except through stdout.

bank.q: Explain stdin, stdout and stderr with their file descriptors. Describe the redirection operators <, >, >>, 2>, 2>&1 and <<.
outline: stdin is fd 0, stdout is fd 1, stderr is fd 2.
< reads input from a file.
> truncates and writes stdout to a file; >> appends.
2> redirects stderr to a file.
2>&1 sends stderr to the current stdout destination; order matters.
<< word is a here-document.

bank.q: A script run by cron fails at night with no message. Explain how you would find and fix the failure using exit status checks, set -e, set -x, trap and logging.
outline: Reproduce the run and check $? after key commands.
Add explicit tests and error messages.
set -e stops on unchecked failures; note its exceptions.
set -x prints a trace; redirect the trace to a log file.
trap ERR or EXIT logs the failure point.
Check cron environment: PATH, current directory and file permissions.
Fix and retest the script.

bank.q: Compare grep, sed and awk for selecting lines, editing text and summarising fields. Choose a tool for three data-cleaning tasks and justify each choice.
outline: grep selects lines by regular expression.
sed edits each line of a stream, for example substitution or deletion.
awk splits records into fields and supports arithmetic and END summaries.
Pipelines combine the tools.
Choice depends on task: selection, editing or field summary.
Readability and speed guide the choice.

bank.q: Write a menu-driven script using while and case that offers count lines, show first lines and quit; put each action in a function.
outline: while true; do prints the menu and reads choice.
read -r choice reads the input safely.
case "$choice" in runs the selected branch.
Functions implement each action.
break leaves the loop on quit.
A default branch prints a usage message.

bank.q: A pipeline processes filenames that contain spaces and sometimes fails to split fields correctly. Diagnose the quoting and IFS problems and show a corrected pipeline.
outline: Unquoted $file splits on IFS and can glob.
Use while IFS= read -r line; do ... done with quoted "$line".
find -print0 with xargs -0 handles spaces safely.
Avoid parsing ls output.
Quote all variable expansions.
Test with filenames containing spaces.

glossary.def: First line #!interpreter in a script; the kernel uses it to choose the interpreter.
Word passed to a command after its name; inside scripts it is available as a positional parameter.
Text beginning with # that the shell ignores, except inside quotes or a here-document.
Replacing $name or ${name} by the variable's value.
After expansion, unquoted results are split into words using characters in IFS.
Shell pathname expansion that replaces patterns containing *, ? or [ ] with matching filenames.
Internal Field Separator; characters used for word splitting and for read to divide fields.
Variable exported to child processes; it appears in their environment.
Variable declared with local in a function; visible in that function and its called functions, not in the parent shell.
Builtin [ or test that evaluates a condition and returns exit status 0 if true.
Short for else if; tests another condition after a failed if branch.
Loop that runs while its condition command returns non-zero; stops when it returns 0.
Loop that assigns each word from a list to a variable and runs the body once per word.
Loop control command that leaves the nearest enclosing loop.
Loop control command that skips to the next iteration of the nearest enclosing loop.
Shell builtin that ends a function and sets its exit status to the given number.
Shell builtin that ends the current shell or script with a status.
Standard input, file descriptor 0; default source of input for commands.
Standard output, file descriptor 1; default destination for normal command output.
Standard error, file descriptor 2; default destination for error messages.
Integer handle for an open file or stream; 0, 1 and 2 are the standard descriptors.
Filter that copies stdin to stdout and to one or more files.
Bash option set -o pipefail; a pipeline's status is the rightmost non-zero status, or zero if all succeed.
Shell builtin that runs a command when the shell receives a signal or exits.
In awk, FS; the input character or regular expression that divides each record into fields $1, $2, ...
Pattern language for matching text; used by grep, sed, awk and shell case patterns.
